title: Complex biological forms come from growth rules, not selection-driven constraints

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Complex biological forms come from growth rules, not selection-driven constraints

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Natural selection can produce forms determined by constraint satisfaction only when those forms are rather simple; complex biological forms are associated instead with explicit evolution rules, mostly those governing the growth of an individual organism.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: when more complex forms are seen they once again tend to be associated not with constraints but rather with the effects of explicit evolution rules—mostly those governing the growth of an individual organism.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 7, “Mechanisms in Programs and Nature”; section “Origins of Simple Behavior” (from p. 351), p. 351. Scope: biological forms shaped by natural selection and development

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch07-19: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.28

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Morphology and phylogeny data exist, but the central causal attribution is generally absent. Retrospective associations cannot cleanly distinguish selection from developmental mechanisms because both jointly shape traits. Resolving the broad claim would require targeted developmental and fitness measurements across many lineages.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Classify biological forms by quantified structural complexity and reconstruct whether each trait arose chiefly through selection on a functional constraint or through developmental growth dynamics. The claim predicts that selection-dominated constraint solutions occupy only the low-complexity range, whereas complex forms trace to explicit developmental rules.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Constraint satisfaction, growth-rule causation, and form complexity are difficult to separate.

Existing comparative data rarely identify the causal contribution of selection versus development.

The dichotomy is not exhaustive.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Model-organism genetics can show that particular complex structures are built by explicit developmental programs, which tests the claim on a restricted set of forms. It does not decide that selection produces constraint-satisfying forms only when they are simple, because both descriptions can be fitted to the same outcome. The scope across biological forms is far wider than the cases with a known mechanism.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Classify biological forms by a pre-registered complexity measure and ask whether the developmental mechanism is a measured growth process or an optimality condition, using known gene-regulatory and morphogenetic data. Complex forms whose construction is a described growth program, and simple forms that match a constraint, would support the split; complex forms that are reached as optima without a growth program would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Developmental mechanisms are known in depth for few organisms.

Simple and complex are not stable categories, and many forms can be described both as growth and as satisfying a constraint.
